core: Working definition of primary prevention, attributed to the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021): measures directed at lowering the prevalence of risk factors common to a range of diseases (tobacco and alcohol use, obesity, high blood pressure) to prevent the initial occurrence of a disorder, including actions that inhibit environmental, economic, and social conditions known to increase those risks
The idea: intervening before the first case, with an original example

The four named tools of primary prevention: vaccination, healthy habits, safety measures, and sanitation, each with one line and an original example (vaccination depth owned by the vaccination sibling topic)
Primary prevention vs the other levels: before onset vs after (secondary and tertiary each get one line of contrast; depth owned by sibling topics)
Who does it: individuals, communities, and policy, each named with one line
The honest note: primary prevention is invisible when it works
The honest framing: primary prevention is the work that makes other care unnecessary
supporting: WHO fact sheet evidence that sanitation is linked to cholera, dysentery, typhoid, intestinal worms, and polio, and that better water, sanitation, and hygiene prevent child deaths
WHO fact sheet evidence that tobacco use, physical inactivity, harmful alcohol use, and unhealthy diets raise the risk of noncommunicable diseases
WHO fact sheet evidence that injuries result from road traffic crashes, falls, drowning, burns, and poisoning
MedlinePlus evidence that vaccines teach the immune system to recognize and defend against harmful germs
CDC evidence that many chronic diseases are caused by a short list of risk behaviors
CDC MMWR list of ten great public health achievements, showing vaccination, motor-vehicle safety, and sanitation as quiet prevention victories
APHA's description of public health as prevention through the organized efforts and informed choices of society, organizations, communities, and individuals
outOfScope: The full prevention framework across all three levels (sibling topic public-health:foundations:prevention)
Secondary prevention in depth: screening mechanics, early detection programs (sibling topic public-health:foundations:secondary-prevention)
Tertiary prevention in depth: disease management, rehabilitation (sibling topic public-health:foundations:tertiary-prevention)
Vaccination in depth: mechanism, schedules, programs, community immunity (sibling topic public-health:foundations:vaccination)
Health promotion strategy in depth (sibling topic public-health:foundations:health-promotion)
Risk measurement and exposure mechanics (sibling topic public-health:foundations:risk)

claims.claim: The WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021) describes primary prevention as directed at lowering the prevalence of risk factors common to a range of diseases (such as tobacco and alcohol use, obesity, and high blood pressure) in order to prevent the initial occurrence of a disorder, and as including actions that inhibit environmental, economic, and social conditions known to increase those risks.

The same WHO glossary defines disease prevention overall as measures to reduce the occurrence of risk factors, prevent the occurrence of disease, arrest its progress, and reduce its consequences once established — the arc within which primary prevention is the before-onset stage.

The same WHO glossary describes secondary prevention as early detection of existing disease, for example through screening and routine health checks, and tertiary prevention as disease management strategies and/or rehabilitation intended to avoid or reduce deterioration or complications from established disease.

Vaccines are injections, liquids, pills, or nasal sprays that teach the body's immune system to recognize and defend against harmful germs, protecting people against serious diseases before they get sick; immunity from a vaccine is safer than immunity gained by getting sick.

Poor sanitation is linked to transmission of diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera and dysentery, as well as typhoid, intestinal worm infections, and polio; better water, sanitation, and hygiene could prevent deaths among children under five (an estimated 395,000 such deaths in 2019).
Tobacco use, physical inactivity, the harmful use of alcohol, unhealthy diets, and air pollution all increase the risk of dying from a noncommunicable (chronic) disease.

Injuries result from road traffic crashes, falls, drowning, burns, poisoning, and violence; unintentional injuries kill an estimated 3.16 million people each year globally, and injury-related deaths total about 4.4 million a year, nearly 8% of all deaths.
Many chronic diseases in the United States are caused by a short list of risk behaviors: tobacco use, poor nutrition, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol use.

Vaccination, motor-vehicle safety, safer workplaces, control of infectious diseases (from clean water and improved sanitation), and safer foods are among CDC's ten great public health achievements of 1900-1999; since 1900 the average American lifespan lengthened by more than 30 years, about 25 of them attributable to public health advances — most of them quiet prevention victories.

Public health promotes and protects the health of all people and their communities and aims to prevent people from getting sick or injured in the first place; the APHA (Winslow-tradition) description names the organized efforts and informed choices of society, organizations, communities, and individuals, and APHA lists worker safety standards, school nutrition programs, and seat-belt and smoke-free-air laws among public health's preventive work.

conflictingEvidence: Sources differ on where primary prevention ends: the WHO glossary frames it around lowering risk factors (behaviour change advice) plus actions that inhibit environmental, economic, and social conditions, while some CDC and consumer materials use 'prevention' loosely to include early detection. The lesson attributes the working definition to WHO, keeps the before-onset boundary strict, and leaves screening to the secondary-prevention sibling topic.

'Prevention is cheaper than treatment' is a widely stated public health argument rather than a single sourced statistic. The lesson keeps any cost claim qualitative — the honest framing is that prevented cases need no care at all — and does not invent a dollar figure.

Vaccination is simultaneously one of primary prevention's tools and a topic of its own. The lesson names it as one tool with a single line and explicitly defers mechanism, schedules, and community immunity to the vaccination sibling topic, avoiding duplication.
unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated phase-4 draft contained no sourced factual claims: its definition ('Primary Prevention is a foundational concept in Public Health'), objectives ('Define primary prevention using course-appropriate language'), and worked example were generic boilerplate with no evidence support and were replaced wholesale with source-verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's boilerplate definition with the WHO Health Promotion Glossary of Terms (2021) definition of primary prevention, paraphrased and attributed.

Replaced the draft's vague objectives with six objectives tied to the verified definition, the before-the-first-case idea, the four named tools, the level contrast, the who-does-it framing, and the honest note/framing.

Added original examples throughout (construction harnesses, playground surfacing, courier cycling, loading-dock gates, village drainage pipe, sunscreen/skin exam/melanoma, cutting board, speed bumps, smoke detectors) — none reused from the prevention sibling lesson.
Expanded the draft's two-subsection college version into seven subsections covering the full required core, all within the simple word band.
Rebuilt the five-question bank around source-verified content with answer keys spread across A/B/C/D (two C-slot and one D-slot keys).
rightsIssues: No rights issues. All facts are synthesized in original prose; the WHO glossary and APHA pages are reference-only (definitions paraphrased and attributed, no wording reproduced), and the CDC pages and MedlinePlus are U.S. government works (public domain).

sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-22 via a Wayback Machine capture (20221228121132) of the English PDF (apps.who.int/iris/rest/bitstreams/1398462/retrieve); canonical who.int URL registered. Supports verbatim: primary prevention is directed towards lowering the prevalence of risk factors common to a range of diseases (tobacco and alcohol use, obesity and high blood pressure) to prevent the initial occurrence of a disorder, and may include actions that inhibit environmental, economic and social conditions known to increase these risks; secondary prevention = early detection of existing disease (screening, routine health checks); tertiary prevention = disease management strategies and/or rehabilitation for established disease. Definitions paraphrased in original prose with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: Vaccines (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: vaccines are injections, liquids, pills, or nasal sprays that teach the body's immune system to recognize and defend against harmful germs; vaccines protect against serious diseases (flu, COVID-19, tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis); immunity from a vaccine is safer than immunity by getting sick; community immunity concept. Used for the one-line vaccination tool in the lesson; mechanism and schedule depth intentionally left to the vaccination sibling topic.

sourceRecords.title: Sanitation (fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: poor sanitation is linked to transmission of diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera and dysentery, as well as typhoid, intestinal worm infections and polio; diarrhoea is largely preventable; better water, sanitation, and hygiene could prevent deaths among children under 5 (395,000 in 2019); 1.4 million people die each year from inadequate drinking-water, sanitation, and hygiene. Figures carry their stated vintage; the lesson keeps the child-death figure dated and qualitative elsewhere.

sourceRecords.title: Injuries and violence (fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: injuries result from road traffic crashes, falls, drowning, burns, poisoning, and violence; unintentional injuries kill an estimated 3.16 million people per year and injury-related deaths total about 4.4 million per year, nearly 8% of all deaths; for people aged 5-29 three of the top five causes of death are injury-related. Used to ground the safety-measures tool of primary prevention.

sourceRecords.title: Noncommunicable diseases (fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: tobacco use, physical inactivity, the harmful use of alcohol, unhealthy diets, and air pollution increase the risk of dying from an NCD; NCDs (chronic diseases) tend to be of long duration; unhealthy diets and lack of physical activity show up as raised blood pressure, raised blood glucose, elevated blood lipids, and obesity. Used for the healthy-habits tool of primary prevention.

sourceRecords.title: About Chronic Diseases
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
sourceRecords.notes: Reused registry record (verified 2026-08-22 via Wayback capture of the canonical CDC URL; cdc.gov blocks direct fetch). Supports: many chronic diseases are caused by a short list of risk behaviors (tobacco use, poor nutrition, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol use); chronic diseases are leading causes of death and disability in the United States and leading drivers of health care costs. Corroborates the healthy-habits tool.

sourceRecords.title: Ten Great Public Health Achievements — United States, 1900-1999 (MMWR Weekly, April 2, 1999 / 48(12);241-243)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
sourceRecords.notes: Reused registry record (verified 2026-08-22 via Wayback capture). Supports: the ten great public health achievements list (vaccination; motor-vehicle safety; safer workplaces; control of infectious diseases; safer and healthier foods; fluoridation of drinking water; recognition of tobacco use as a health hazard, among others); control of infectious diseases resulted from clean water and improved sanitation, dramatically reducing waterborne typhoid and cholera; since 1900 the average American lifespan lengthened by more than 30 years, about 25 years attributable to public health advances. Anchors the honest note (invisible when it works) and the honest framing.
